Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 86, verses 1–2:

Surat al-Tariq

It is Meccan without disagreement, and it has seventeen verses according to the well-known count, while in al-Taysir it is counted as sixteen. When, in what precedes it, God, glorified is He, mentioned the disbelievers' denial of the Qur'an, He here draws attention to the lowliness of man. Then, exalted is He, He digressed from this to a description of the Qur'an. Then He, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, to give those deniers respite. So He, mighty and majestic is He, said: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿By the sky﴾: it is the well-known sky, as the majority hold. It was also said that here it means rain, which is one of its usages, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"When the sky descends upon the land of a people, we graze upon it, even if they are angry."
/ Its state is not hidden.

﴿And the Knocker-by-night (al-Tariq)﴾: it is in origin an active participle from al-tarq, meaning striking with a blow whose force produces a sound, and from it come al-mitraqa (the hammer) and al-tariq (the road), because travellers knock upon it (tatruquha). Then in the common usage of the language it became a name for one who travels the road, on the notion that he strikes it with his foot, and it became so well known for this that it became a literal meaning. Then it was specialised to one who comes at night, because in most cases he finds the doors closed and knocks on them. Then it broadened to include everything that appears by night, whatever it may be, even the imaginary forms that appear in it; and the Arabs describe these as "coming at night" (turuq), as in the poet's saying:

"The phantom came knocking, and not like a traveller by night, who comes with his baggage and does not turn aside."

What is meant by it here, according to the majority, is the star that appears at night, either as a generic noun or as a specific known star, as you will learn, God willing. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what the Knocker-by-night is?﴾ is an exalting of its status following its magnification by the oath, and an indication that its elevation is such that the perception of created beings cannot reach it, so it must be received from the Creator, the All-Knowing. So the first "ma" is a subject (mubtada') and "adraka" is its predicate, and the second "ma" is a predicate, and "al-Tariq" is a subject, according to what some of the verifiers have chosen; that is: what has informed you what the Knocker-by-night is?

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 86, verse 3:**

His statement, glorified is He: ﴿The piercing star﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*) of a deleted subject (*mubtada'*), and the sentence is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) that came as an answer to a question arising from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What is it?" Then it was said: "It is the star, etc..." And *al-thaqib* (the piercing) originally means that which pierces, then it came to mean the shining one, based on the conception that it pierces the darkness. It may be restricted to stars and shooting stars for this reason, and on the conception that its light penetrates the celestial spheres (*aflak*) and the like. Al-Farra' said: *al-thaqib* means the elevated, as one says: "The bird *thaqaba*," meaning it rose and ascended. The intended meaning of "the piercing star" is the genus (*jins*) according to al-Hasan, for every star certainly has a piercing light, and likewise every elevated star, and the variation in this is not harmful. Others held that the intended meaning is a specific, known star. From Ibn 'Abbas it is reported that it is the Jadi (the Pole Star). Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd that it is the Thurayya (the Pleiades), which the Arabs apply the name "star" to specifically. It is also related from him that it is Zuhal (Saturn), which is the furthest and highest of the wandering stars (*sayyarat*), and whose light pierces more of the celestial spheres, according to what the earlier astrologers (*munajjimun*) claim. We said "the furthest of the wandering stars" because the Jadi and the Thurayya are, according to them, far further than it, and likewise according to the moderns. From al-Farra' it is reported that it is the Moon, because it is the sign of the night and the brightest of the stars in it, and it is the time of its dominion. You know that applying the name "star" to it, even described as such, is not common. It was also said that it is the star called the Morning Star (*kawkab al-subh*).

It is reported from 'Ali, may God honour his face, that it is a star in the seventh heaven which does not dwell there. He then distinguished it: when the stars take their places in the heaven, it descends and is with them, then it returns to its place in the seventh heaven. So it is "the one who knocks" (*tariq*) when it descends and "the one who knocks" when it ascends.

It is not hidden that what is well known is that the one who dwells in the seventh heaven, meaning the seventh sphere alone, is Saturn. This would make it a statement that the piercing star is Saturn. But no descent or ascent is known for it in the commonly understood sense. Also, it is not conceivable for it to descend to where the stars are, meaning the fixed stars, because the known view among them is that they are in the eighth sphere. It is rationally possible that some of them are in spheres above that. Indeed, the moderns stated, on the basis of what was established for them, that they differ in height, and they had no doubt that many of them are far further than Saturn by a great distance. If the apparent meanings are considered, and we say that they are in the lowest heaven though they vary in height, then this too is contradicted by the fact that the stars take their places in the heaven without Saturn being with them. In sum, what undermines this report is much. That 'Ali, may God honour his face, intended another star with such a status is something whose condition is not hidden. What fairness and the abandonment of partisanship require is that the report is a lie attributed to the Commander (*al-Amir*), may God be pleased with him and honour his face. It was also permitted, on the reading that the genus is intended, that it means the genus of shooting stars with which devils are pelted, but this is not the right view. And what is related: "Abu Talib was with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, when a star fell and became full of water, then light. Abu Talib was alarmed and said: 'What is this?'

He, upon him be prayer and peace, said: 'This is a star that was thrown, and it is one of the signs of God, exalted is He.' Abu Talib was amazed, and then this was revealed."

This does not necessitate that, as is not hidden. Ibn 'Atiyya claimed that what is meant by ﴿the one who knocks﴾ is everything that comes knocking of affairs and created things, so it includes the piercing star and other things. The meaning of ﴿And what will make you know what the one who knocks is?﴾ would be the true reality of the one who knocks, the *alif-lam* in ﴿what the one who knocks﴾ being like it in: "You are the man" (*anta al-rajul*). "I do not know what the one who knocks is upon this man," until he rode this difficult path in the interpretation. And in the mention of this at the time of the oath, with an attribute shared between it and others, then the indication that this attribute does not disclose the essence of its matter, and that this is something beyond the reach of creatures' thoughts, then its interpretation as the piercing star is, in glorifying its status and exalting its position, something not hidden from one of penetrating insight. And for the sake of this meaning, He did not initially say "and the piercing star," although that is shorter and clearer. God, mighty and majestic, may glorify the status of whatever He wills of His creation for whatever He wills. There is no indication here of anything that the astrologers claim concerning the stars, Saturn and others, regarding influence on happiness, misery, or the like. And the answer to the oath (*jawab al-qasam*) follows.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 86, verse 4:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is over every soul a guardian﴾. What lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad), brought in for the stated purpose of emphasising the greatness of the thing sworn by, which in turn entails emphasising the content of the sentence sworn to. It has also been said that its response (jawab) is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, He is able to bring him back﴾, and that what lies between is a parenthetical clause; but this, as you see, is [weak]. Here "in" (in) is negating, and "lamma" (lamma) is in the sense of "illa" (except), and its coming in this way
Page 96
is a well-known usage, as Abu Hayyan transmitted from al-Akhfash concerning Hudhayl and others, who say: "I swore upon you, or I asked you, lamma you do such-and-such," meaning "illa you do." By this the objection of al-Jawhari, who denied this usage, was refuted. Al-Radi said: it does not come except after a manifest or implied negation, and it is only used in the "mufarragh" (exclusive construction with no stated object); that is, unlike "illa." "Kull" (every) is for emphasising generality, since its origin is established from an indefinite noun occurring in a negative context. It is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar), according to the well-known view, is "hafiz" (guardian). "Alayha" (over it) is connected to it; and according to what you have heard from al-Radi, [its predicate] is omitted; that is: every soul, in whatever state it may be, is only in the state of there being over it a guardian; that is, one who watches over and oversees, and this is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is ever over all things a watcher﴾.

When you are alone for a day, do not say "I was alone," but say "Over me is a watcher."

It has been said: it is one who guards its deeds from the angels, peace be upon them, and records against it whatever good or evil it earns, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble writers﴾ [and the rest of the verse]... This was narrated from Ibn Sirin, Qatadah and others, and they restricted "soul" to the one who is accountable. It has been said: it refers to him and to whoever is assigned to guard it and defend it from the angels, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him who guard him by the command of Allah﴾.

From Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There are assigned to the believer one hundred and sixty angels who repel from him, as flies are repelled from a bowl of honey. Were the servant left to himself for the blink of an eye, the devils would snatch him away."

It has been said: it is the intellect, which guides a person to his interests and restrains him from his harms.

Most readers recited "lamma" with light (tashdid absent). According to the Kufans, "in" is negating as already mentioned, the "lam" is in the sense of "illa" (except), and "ma" is superfluous. They explicitly state here that "kull" and "hafiz" are subject and predicate, so do not overlook this. According to the Basrans, "in" is a lightened form of the heavy "inna," "kull" is the subject, "ma" is superfluous, and the "lam" is the one introduced to distinguish the negating "in" from the lightened "in." "Hafiz" is the predicate of the subject, and "alayha" is connected to it. A pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n) was assumed, and it was objected that there is no need for it, since in other than the open (maftuha) form it is weak due to the absence of governance, and furthermore it disrupts the introduction of the distinguishing "lam," because when the predicate is a clause, it is preferable to introduce the "lam" on the first part, as stated in al-Tashil, or on the second part, as stated by some scholars in their glosses on it. Perhaps the one who said "i.e., indeed the matter is: every soul, surely over it is a guardian" did not intend to assume the pronoun, but only to explain the resulting meaning. Harun transmitted that it was also read: "inna" with tashdid, "kulla" in the accusative, and "lamma" with lightening; so the "lam" is the one introduced into the predicate of "inna," and "ma" is superfluous. On all readings, the answering force of the oath is evident, since there is the element that the oath is introduced by; its introduction with the heavy form is well known, and with the light form ﴿By Allah, you had nearly brought me to ruin﴾, and with the negating form ﴿Indeed, Allah holds back the two heavens lest they cease﴾.

The words of the Most High, ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾, are a consequence (*mutafarri'*) of what precedes them. The *fa'* is not an elucidatory *fa'* (*fa' fasihah*, one that marks an implied condition), contrary to al-Tibi, since the sentence is sound without positing any omission. This holds whether the watcher (*al-hafiz*) is God, Mighty and Majestic, or the angel whom He, exalted is His majesty, appointed to guard, in the manner you have heard. When He, glorified is He, affirmed that there is over him a watcher from Him, exalted is He, He urged him to the reflection that makes this known, together with its attributes, as if it were said: let the one over whom it is watching come to know Him, through His appointing the watcher or through Himself, and let him know his return to Him, exalted is He, and let him do what will gladden him at the time of return.

He expressed the first (interpretation) by His words, ﴿let him look﴾, to clarify the way that makes it known. It is an elaboration containing brevity, and the last two (meanings) are incorporated into it. And if the intended meaning is the intellect ('*aql*), then, since He, glorified is He, affirmed that he has an intellect that guides him to what is beneficial and restrains him from what is harmful, He urged him to employ it in what benefits him and not to leave it idle or neglect it, as if it were said: let him look with his intellect, and let him reflect with it upon the origin of his creation, until there becomes clear to him the power of the one who bestowed it, and that if He is able to bring him into being from materials that never smelled the scent of life at all, then He, glorified is He, is more able, and more capable, of restoring him; so he will act in the way that will gladden him at the time of restoration. The *tafri'* may be established in a single manner across all the aspects, so reflect.

﴿Mimma khuliqa﴾ is an interrogative. *Min* is connected to *khuliqa*, and the clause is in the position of an accusative object of *yanzur* (look), and it is suspended by the interrogative.

[Page 97]

The words of the Exalted, ﴿Created from a gushing fluid﴾, form a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a sentence that begins a new statement) that answers an implied question, as if it were said: "From what was he created?" So it was said: ﴿Created from a fluid﴾, and so on. The apparent meaning of the words of some of the eminent scholars is that it is an answer to the question mentioned, with the prepositional phrase attached to *yanzur* ("let him look"). There is some looseness in this, and it seems that their intent is that it has the form of an answer, and that they treated it as a true answer to that question, on the basis that it is cut off from *yanzur*. This is nothing according to one who has sound judgment.

*Daf'q* (gushing) is pouring with a thrust and flowing quickly. By "gushing fluid" is meant the semen (*mani*). The word *dafiq* has been said to mean *madfuq* (thrust out), by interpreting the active participle in the sense of the passive. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read it that way. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said that it is in the form of a relative adjective (*nasab*), like *laban* (having milk) and *tamir* (having dates), meaning "possessing a thrust," and it applies to both the active and the passive. It has also been said that it is an active participle, and its attribution to the water is metaphorical (*majaz*). The attribute of its companion has been attributed to it for emphasis. Or it is a concealed metaphor (*isti'ara makniyya*) and imaginative metaphor (*isti'ara takhyiliyya*), as al-Sakkaki held. Or it is an explicit metaphor (*isti'ara musarrah*) by describing it as gushing, because its drops follow one another, as if it were gushing, that is, some of it thrusts the other part.

Ibn 'Atiyya explained *daf'q* as thrusting, saying: "*Daf'q* is the water thrusting some of itself against other parts of itself. One says: 'The valley and the torrent gushed' when they come, riding one another. It is valid that the water is gushing, because some of it thrusts the rest, so some of it is gushing and some of it is gushed." Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that *daf'q* in the sense of thrusting is not transmitted in the lexicon; rather, what is transmitted is that it means pouring. He related from al-Layth that *dafaqa* means "poured out at once," so *dafiq* means "poured out," and there is no need for interpretation. This was criticized on the ground that al-Layth stood alone in this, as is stated in al-Qamus and elsewhere.

It has been said: "from water," though a human is not created except from two waters, the water of the man and the water of the woman. For this reason the creation of 'Isa, peace be upon him, was outside the normal custom, because what is meant here is the mixture of the two waters in the womb, and by their mixing they become one water. Its description as gushing has been said to refer to one of its two components, which is the man's semen. It has also been said that it refers to both, and the woman's semen is also gushing toward the womb. This indicates that the mixed fluid is intended, according to what has been said.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 86, verse 7:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It comes forth from between the loins﴾, meaning: from between the bones of the loins (ṣulb) of every man, that is, his back. ﴿And the breastbones﴾, meaning: and from between the breastbones (tarā'ib) of every woman, that is, the bones of her chest, the plural of tarība. It has also been explained as the place of the necklace on the chest. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is a singular for each woman, but it is pluralised, as in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Slender, fair, not overly fleshy, her breastbones polished like a mirror (sajanjal).

This is taken in view of what surrounds it, as stated in al-Bahr. It also occurs in the singular, tarīb, as in the saying of al-Muthaqqab al-'Abdi:

And of gold that shows upon a tarīb, like the colour of ivory, free of wrinkles.

The interpretation of the verse in the sense mentioned has been related from Sufyan and Qatada, except that both of them said: meaning, it comes forth from between the loins of the man and the breastbones of the woman. Its apparent sense, like the verse, is that one of the two ends is the loins and the other is the breastbones, which is other than what we have said. On this basis it has been said: it is like your saying, "Much good comes forth from between Zayd and 'Amr," meaning that they are both causes of it. It has also been said that this is in view of the fact that the man and the woman become like a single thing, so the loins and the breastbones are as of one person. So consider this carefully. Then, what has preceded is based either on the view that the breastbones are specific to the woman, as is the apparent sense of the words of more than one scholar, or on taking its definite article as referring to a known thing (al-'ahd).

Al-Hasan (and it is also related from Qatada) said: the meaning is: it comes forth from between the loins of each of the man and the woman, and the breastbones of each of them. He did not specify the breastbones. It was said: the bones of the chest. It was said: what is between the two breasts. It was said: what is between the shoulder-blades and the chest. It was said: the collarbones. It was said: four ribs on the right side of the chest and four on its left. It is related from Ibn Jubayr: the ribs that are at the lower end of the spine. Makki related from Ibn 'Abbas that they are the extremities of a person: his two legs, his two hands and his two eyes. However, the most well-known view is that they are the bones of the chest and the place of the necklace on it.

This has been criticised, as the Imam [al-Razi] said, by some of the heretics (may God humble them) on the grounds that semen is only generated from the residue of the fourth digestion, and it is separated from all parts of the body, so it takes from each limb a nature and a property, prepared to generate those limbs from it. If what is meant is that the majority of the components of semen are generated in those two places, then this is weak, because most of it is generated in the brain. Do you not see that in its form it resembles the brain, and that one who indulges in it first shows weakness in his brain and his eyes? If what is meant is that its place of rest is there, then this too is weak, because its place of rest is veins that wind round one another near the two testicles, and these are called the vessels of semen. If what is meant is that its place of exit is there, this too is so, because the senses indicate otherwise.

He (may God have mercy on him) replied that there is no doubt that the most helpful of the organs in the generation of semen is the brain, and its deputy, the spinal cord, in the loins, and branches descending to the front of the body, which are the tarība. Therefore these two were singled out for mention. Moreover, their statements about the matter of semen and its generation are pure supposition and weak conjecture, while the Glorious Word of God, falsehood does not come to it from before it or from behind it, is the one accepted and relied upon. End quote.

In al-Kashf I say: the spinal cord lies between the loins and the breastbones, and there is no need to restrict tarība to women. The descending branches may prevent this, since those branches, if they are such, are nerves and not hollow channels. The correct view, and God knows best, is that the spinal cord, the faculties of the brain, the heart and the liver all cooperate in bringing forth that residue in the state in which it is fit to become the origin of the person, as is explained in its proper place.

His words, glory be to Him: ﴿from between the loins and the breastbones﴾ is a concise expression comprising the influence of three organs. The breastbones include the heart and the liver, and their inclusion of the heart is more evident. The loins are the spinal cord, and through it the brain. Perhaps there is no need to alert to the location of the liver, because it is evident, as it is ripe blood. Only what is hidden needed mentioning, namely the role of the brain and the heart in the formation of that water, so their locations were pointed out. It has been said: the beginning of its exit is from there, just as its end is at the urethra. End quote. It has also been said: if what is between the loins and the breastbones is taken as a metonymy for the whole body, it would not be far-fetched, and their specific mention would be because they are like a receptacle for the heart, which is the great lump of flesh within it. The matter of this metonymy, as Makki related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the breastbones, is more evident.

Some have claimed that it is permissible for the loins and the breastbones to belong to the man; that is, it comes forth from between the loins of every man and his breastbones. Then by "the gushing water" is meant only the man's water, and the speech is either taken as a case of predominance (taghlīb) or on the basis that the woman has no water at all, let alone gushing water, as has been said. What is in this is not hidden. The claim that the woman has no water is refuted by the Sharia and other sources.

Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ibn Muqsim read: «yukhraju» in the passive voice. These two are of the people of Makkah. 'Isa read: «al-ṣulub» with a ḍamma on the ṣād and the lām, and al-Yamani with a fatḥa on both. On both dialects is related the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

Broad of bones, large of the hollow of the throat, in a loin like a well-polished sheet of... (al-'anān al-mu'addam).

There is also a fourth dialect in it, ṣālib, as in the saying of al-'Abbas:

He moved from a ṣālib to a womb.

This form is rarely used. Some eminent scholars cited His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He was created from gushing water﴾, as evidence that the human being is the specific bodily structure, as the majority of theologians hold, who deny the rational human soul that is immaterial and is neither within the body nor outside it. He said: this is a strong proof for that. Its interpretation requires the omission of a modifier, that is, the creation of the human body. It is not heard unless there is a proof that its apparent meaning is impossible. End quote.

You know that those who hold to the immaterial rational soul have set forth proofs for its establishment in their own view. Yes, there are discussions in it by those who deny it, and a full verification of this, beyond which nothing more is needed, is in the book al-Ruh by the scholar Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 86, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, He is able to return him.﴾ The first pronoun refers to the Creator, exalted is His majesty. And just as He magnified (the matter) at first by omitting the agent in His saying, ﴿From what was he created?﴾ ﴿He was created﴾, since no one could be thought of as creator other than Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, He magnified it a second time by using the pronoun. The second pronoun refers to the human being; that is: indeed, He who originated his creation from what has been mentioned is able to return him after his death, to clarify the power. This is like the saying of the poet:

Even if the cold of its fangs, high (in position), is (too) poor (to help me), I am indeed poor.

For he intended to clarify the poverty, since otherwise its mention would not be correct when set against "more poor than me," and (it is) an emphatic affirmation in wording for what the clear proof has established in meaning. For this reason, (the word) "qadir" (able) here is explained as making power clear, as in al-Kashshaf. It also takes into account the sense of restriction, so he said: that is, "able" over His returning him specifically, and it seems that this is because the purpose for which the speech is directed is that matter; so it is as if anything other than it is set aside in relation to it. In that case, what has been mentioned is intended: making the preposition (min) part of the complement of "qadir," or taking it as indicating its relative (clause) according to the two views. And the separation of the sentence from what preceded it is because it is the answer to the interrogative, not the part before it. Mujahid and Ikrimah said:

The second pronoun refers to the water; that is: indeed, He, may He be exalted, is able to return the water into the urethra or into the loins. And it is not something (correct). Similar to this is the meaning if it refers to the human being: that He, may He be majestic and exalted, returns him from old age to youth, is able, as has been narrated from al-Dahhak. What we have mentioned first is narrated from Ibn Abbas.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 86, verse 9:

﴿On the Day when the secrets are tested﴾. That is: what is concealed in the hearts of beliefs and intentions and other things, and what is hidden of deeds, is investigated and examined, and what is good among them is distinguished from what is corrupt. The root meaning of ibtila' (testing) is ikhtibar (examination), and its application to what has been mentioned is an application to the necessary consequence. Taking "the secrets" in its general sense is the apparent meaning.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ata' and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir that they are: the fast, the prayer, and the ghusl from janabah (ritual impurity).

Al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Shu'ab from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted has guaranteed four things for His creation: the prayer, the zakat, the fast of Ramadan, and the ghusl from janabah, and these are the secrets of which Allah the Exalted said: ﴿On the Day when the secrets are tested﴾."

In al-Bahr, he added tawhid to them, and perhaps the purpose is to explain their greatness by way of exaggeration, not the literal restriction. Al-Hasan heard someone reciting the verse of al-Ahwas:

"There will remain for her, in the hidden depths of the heart and the inner self, a secret of love, on the Day when the secrets are tested."

He said: "How heedless he is of what is in (al-Sama' wal-Tariq)." It seems he understood "remaining" in it as meaning not being known at all. So let it be understood. "Yawma" (on the day), according to a group of skilled grammarians, is an adverb of time governing a verb omitted but indicated by it; that is: "He returns him on the day..." etc. Al-Zamakhshari and a group said: it is an adverb of time governing "rij'ihi" (his returning), and it was objected that this involves separating the verbal noun from its object by a foreign element. It was answered, on one hand, that this is permissible because of their latitude with adverbs, and on the other, that the intervening element here is not foreign, since it is either an explanation or a governing element according to both views. 'Isam al-Din said: separating by this foreign element is as if there were no separation, because the object is intended to be placed before it, and it was only postponed for the sake of observing the rhyme (fasila). In this there is what is not hidden.

It was also said: it is an adverb of time governing "nasir" (a helper) afterwards, and Abu Hayyan objected that this is invalid, because what follows the fa' cannot govern what precedes it, and likewise the negating particle ma, according to the well-known and preferred view. It was also said: it is an object of an omitted "udhkur" (remember), and that is as you see. It is specified as this, or what precedes it, according to the opinion of Mujahid and Ikrimah. Al-Dahhak held the two preceding views mentioned just above. Al-Tabarsi permitted its being connected to "qadir" (able), but the majority of grammarians did not connect it to it, because it gives the impression that Allah's power, Mighty and Majestic is He, is restricted to one day and not another, as more than one scholar has said.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: They avoided having the governing element be "laqadir" (surely able) because of the necessity of restricting power to that day alone. But if one reflects on the meaning and what the eloquent speech of the Arabs requires, it is permissible for it to be the governing element, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Surely He is able to return him﴾ absolutely, or at the end, and at every time. Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned, of the times, the greatest time for the disbelievers, because it is the time of recompense and of reaching punishment, so that people gather in fear of it and dread of it. End of quotation. And this, despite what is in it, does not remove the implication.

﴿So he has no ﴾ power ﴿of his own﴾, meaning the human being, by which he could defend himself, ﴿nor any helper﴾ whom he could rely on for victory. ﴿By the sky﴾, which is the canopy according to the majority (al-jumhur) opinion, ﴿which returns﴾, meaning the rain, also according to their view, as in the verse of al-Khansa':

On the day of parting you see tears flowing,
like the rain (al-rajʿ) of a night-cloud that drifts onward.

Its origin is the verbal noun of rajaʿa, whether transitive or intransitive, according to one view. Its specific verbal noun is al-ruju'. They named the rain thus, just as they called it al-awb, the verbal noun of āba. From this is the saying of the poet:

A high, lofty land, which none seeks shelter in for its remoteness,
except the clouds, the rains, and the torrents.

Page 100
So that it returns, or because the cloud carries it from the seas of the earth and then returns it to the earth. Many have built this on the (popular) assumption, but there is a discussion about it. As for ʿan in the sense of aw (أو), the intended meaning of al-rajʿ here is the bee (al-naḥl), because God Most High returns it (the honey) from time to time. Al-Hasan said: it is so named because it returns with provision every year. Or they intended this as an omen (tafāʾul). Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid interpreted al-sama' as the clouds and al-rajʿ as the rain. Ibn Zayd said: "al-sama'" is the well-known (sky), and "al-rajʿ" is the return of the sun, the moon, and the stars from one state to another and from one station to another within it, and before their return itself, for they return in every cycle to the point from which they began to move. This is based on the premise that the sky and the celestial sphere (al-falak) are one, so that it moves, and its apogee becomes its perigee and its perigee becomes its apogee. You have already heard, in what preceded, that the apparent words of the early scholars (al-salaf) indicate that the sky is other than the celestial sphere and that it does not revolve or move; what was mentioned is the opinion of the philosophers (al-falasifa) and those who followed them. It was also said: "al-rajʿ" refers to the angels, peace be upon them, who were so named because they return with the deeds of the servants.

﴿By the earth that splits open﴾: it is what the earth splits open with of vegetation, and its root meaning is splitting. The term was applied to vegetation by way of majaz (figurative usage). Or it is a verbal noun (masdar) derived from the passive form (al-mabni lil-maf'ul), so the meaning is its being split open by vegetation. This was narrated from 'Atiyyah and Ibn Zayd. It was also said: its being split open by springs. This was objected to on the grounds that describing the heaven and the earth when swearing by them matches the reality of the Qur'an, which speaks of resurrection, through the two attributes mentioned, to indicate that they themselves are among its evidences. This is the secret behind expressing rain as "return" (raj'), and it refers to the earth's splitting open with plants, which imitates resurrection, as mentioned in several places of the Revelation, not to its splitting open by springs. From this is known what is wrong in interpreting "return" as other than rain. Likewise, what is in Mujahid's statement about ﴿al-Sad'﴾: what is in the earth of cracks, valleys, trenches, and splitting by tilling and other things. And what is also narrated from him: "al-Sad': the paths split open by walkers." It was also said: "possessing the dead," because they split open from them for resurrection.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 86, verses 13–14:

﴿Indeed, it﴾ i.e., the Qur'an, of which these verses are a part, which speak of the beginning of man's state and his return (to God). This is preferable to taking the pronoun as referring to what preceded; i.e., what I have told you of My power to bring you back to life, because the Qur'an treats that matter primarily. And His saying, ﴿it is indeed a decisive word﴾, is more fitting with it. The meaning is: a word that separates truth from falsehood, having reached the utmost extent in that, so that it is as if it were the very essence of decisiveness. It has also been said: the contrast of decisiveness with jest that follows requires that it be interpreted as "decisive" in the sense of "definitive"; i.e., a word that is definitively settled. The first (interpretation) is better.

﴿And it is not a jest﴾, i.e., there is not in any part of it any trace of jest; rather all of it is pure earnestness. So it is fitting that the misguided be guided by it, and that the necks of the tyrants submit to it.

In a hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhi, al-Darimi and Ibn al-Anbari, from al-Harith al-A'war, from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed, there will be a trial (fitnah).' I said: 'What is the way out of it, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'The Book of Allah. In it is the news of those before you, the report of what comes after you, and the judgment of what is among you. It is the decisive word, not a jest. Whoever abandons it out of arrogance, Allah will break him. Whoever seeks guidance in other than it, Allah will lead him astray. It is the firm rope of Allah, it is the Wise Reminder, it is the Straight Path. It is that which whims do not deviate from, that which scholars never tire of, that which tongues do not get confused by, that which does not wear out through repetition, and whose wonders never end. It is that which the jinn did not refrain from, when they heard it, from saying: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾ ﴿which guides to righteousness﴾. Whoever speaks by it speaks truly, whoever judges by it is just, whoever acts by it is rewarded, and whoever calls to it is guided to a straight path.'"

In this there is what suffices in refutation of those who cast it behind their backs.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 86, verse 15–16:

﴿Indeed they﴾ i.e., the disbelievers of Makkah.

﴿are plotting a plot﴾ they are devising schemes to nullify His affair and extinguish His light, or to nullify the affair of God Most High and extinguish the light of the Truth. The first is more coherent in its arrangement, while this one is said to yield greater benefit.

﴿a [great] plot﴾ i.e., a great one, to the extent their power allows. The sentence may be an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: "If the condition of the Qur'an is what has been mentioned, what is the condition of those who say about it what they say?" So it was said: ﴿Indeed they are plotting a plot﴾ ﴿and I am plotting a plot﴾, i.e., I confront them with a firm plot that cannot be repelled, since I lead them step by step from where they do not know, or I confront them with My plot in exalting His affair and multiplying His light from where they do not expect. The separation (fasl) is for this purpose. It was also said: [the separation is] lest it be supposed that it is coordinated (conjoined) with the answer to the oath, although it is not the thing sworn to.

﴿So give respite to the disbelievers﴾: do not busy yourself with taking vengeance on them, do not invoke destruction upon them, but be patient and await vengeance upon them, and do not hasten. The *fa'* (فاء, the particle of consequence) indicates that what follows it is a consequence of what precedes it, for the report that He, may He be exalted, is Himself plotting against them and not neglecting them necessarily requires that He grant them respite and that you refrain from confronting their scheming. The placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun serves to censure them as "the father and mother of evil" (أبي الخبائث وأمها), and it has been said that it is to indicate the cause of what the speech contains of threat. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿give them respite﴾ (أمهلهم) is a substitute (*badal*) for *mahhil* (مَهِّلْ), as he stated explicitly in *al-Irshad*. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿gently﴾ (رُوَيْدًا) is either an absolute verbal noun (*masdar*) emphasizing the meaning of the governing verb, or an adjective modifying its omitted verbal noun; that is, "give them respite, a gentle respite," i.e., "a near one," as Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas, or "a little one," as was reported from Qatada. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Suddi that he said: that is, "give them respite until I command the fighting." Perhaps this is what is meant by the respite being near or little. Some scholars chose that what is meant is until the Day of Resurrection, because what happened after the command to fight, like what happened on the day of Badr and in the rest of the military campaigns, did not encompass them all, whereas what will happen on the Day of Resurrection encompasses them. The "nearness" is in view of the fact that everything that is coming is near, and on this same basis the "littleness" (is understood). Moreover, whoever dies, his resurrection has taken place. The apparent meaning, however, is what al-Suddi said, and indeed what befell them after the command to fight befell them. The absence of a true generality does no harm.

*Ruwayd* (رُوَيْدًا), in its origin, as Abu Ubayda said, is the diminutive of *rud* (رُودٍ) with a *damma*, and he recited:

*"As if she were an intoxicated man walking slowly (ʿalā rūd)."*

That is, "slowly" (ʿalā mahl). Abu Hayyan and a group said: it is the diminutive of *irwad* (إرْوادٌ), the verbal noun of *raada* (رَوَدَ) which is *yarood* (يَرُودُ), with apocope (*tarkhim*, تَرْخِيمٌ), and it is a diminutive of diminution and lessening. In usage it has two other aspects: that it is a verb-noun (*ism fiʿl*, اسْمُ فِعْلٍ), as in *ruydan Zaydu* (رَيْدًا زَيْدُ), meaning "give him respite"; and that it is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*, حالٌ), as in *sāra al-qawmu ruwaydan* (سارَ القَوْمُ رُوَيْدًا), meaning "the people went slowly, not hastening." No one mentioned the possibility of it being a verb-noun here, and Ibn al-Shaykh explicitly stated that it does not apply here, giving as the reason that the imperatives are in the sense of... so it is as if it were said: "Give respite to the disbelievers, give them respite." The purpose of emphasis is achieved by the second, so the third is superfluous. There is scrutiny in this reasoning, for emphasis may be employed with expressions that are identical in wording and meaning, as in that.

In the hadith: "Whichever woman marries herself off without a guardian, her marriage is void, void, void."

There is no difference between sentences and single words. Indeed, this is very contrary to the apparent meaning.

May Allah have mercy on him, he permitted it to be a circumstantial accusative, meaning: "give them respite, while not being hastened." The apparent meaning is that it is an emphatic circumstantial accusative, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief﴾. And this too is far-fetched. The apparent sense of the words of Abu Hayyan and others is that the second command is an emphasis of the first. They said: the difference between the two expressions in form is for increasing the consolation of the Prophet (ﷺ) and steadying him. The addition indicates a difference, as if *kallā* (كَلَّا) were an independent utterance commanding deliberateness, so it is stronger than mere repetition.

Ibn Abbas recited: "*mahhilhum*" (مَهِّلْهُمْ), with a fatha on the *mim* and a shadda on the *ha*, in conformity with the wording of the first command.
